body: Investors earn less than the funds they own because they buy after gains and sell after falls. Morningstar measured a gap of about **1.2 points a year** in the US over the ten years to 2025, widening to 2.1 points in the most volatile funds ([Morningstar](https://www.morningstar.com/business/insights/research/mind-the-gap-2025)). In India, Axis MF found equity and hybrid funds returned about **19.1% a year from 2003 to 2022 while the average investor earned about 13.8%** ([Axis MF](https://www.axismf.com/cms/sites/default/files/pdf-factsheets/Thinking%20Aloud%20-%20Using%20your%20Mutual%20Funds%20More%20Effectively.pdf)). Over 30 years, that gap compounds to roughly a 4x difference in ending wealth. Even Lynch's investors lagged him: one estimate puts their dollar-weighted return at 13.4% against the fund's 21.8% over 1981–1990 ([CBS MoneyWatch](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/lessons-from-a-great-fund-managers-record)). Barber and Odean found the most active fifth of traders netted 11.4% a year against 18.5% for the least active, with gross returns similar, so costs ate the difference ([Odean](https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/odean/Papers%20current%20versions/Individual_Investor_Performance_Final.pdf)). Investors also sell winners too early and hold losers too long, and the winners they sell go on to beat the losers they keep ([Odean, 1998](https://faculty.haas.berkeley.edu/odean/papers/disposition/disposition.html)).

**Mohnish Pabrai (*The Dhandho Investor*, 2007)**
- **The nine principles.** They include investing in existing businesses, simple businesses, distressed businesses in distressed industries, businesses with durable moats, few bets/big bets/infrequent bets, arbitrage, margin of safety, and "low risk, high uncertainty." — [Manas Saloi book summary](https://manassaloi.com/booksummaries/2016/03/14/mohnish-pabrai-the-dhandho-investor.html); [GuruFocus](https://www.gurufocus.com/news/338613/the-dhandho-framework)
- **Asymmetry (said).** "Heads I win; tails I don't lose much." — [Outlook Money](https://www.outlookmoney.com/invest/mohnish-pabrais-lessons-in-the-dhandho-of-investing)
- **Cloning (said).** Pabrai calls himself a "shameless cloner" of Buffett, Munger and others. — [Antoine Buteau, lessons from Pabrai](https://www.antoinebuteau.com/lessons-from-mohnish-pabrai/)
- **Evolution (commentary).** Later commentary says his approach has shifted toward growth with a value bent. — [Outlook Money](https://www.outlookmoney.com/invest/mohnish-pabrais-lessons-in-the-dhandho-of-investing)

**Terry Smith (Fundsmith)**
- **Mantra (said).** "Buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing." Fundsmith: "We only buy shares in good companies, try not to overpay and then do nothing." — [Fundsmith](https://www.fundsmith.co.uk/news/2015/2171-this-is-money-firms-which-provide-good-products-or-services-are-key-to-investing-says-fundsmith-boss/); [Smithson/Fidelity "three steps"](https://smithson.co.uk/news/2015/2036-fidelity-three-steps-to-heaven)
- **Primary test.** The key test is a high ROCE across the economic cycle. Holdings typically earn 25–30% ROCE. — [Trustnet](https://www.trustnet.com/news/662915/three-simple-steps-to-making-returns-like-terry-smith)
- **Conflicting thresholds.** Blogs cite 15–20% or "20%+" ROCE, and one lists interest coverage >15x. These are lower-quality secondary sources. — [MarketScreener](https://in.marketscreener.com/news/latest/Legendary-investor-Terry-Smith-44733685)
- Fundsmith's annual owner letters also stress high gross margins, high cash conversion and a FCF yield-based valuation [primary, not re-fetched].

body:
`strategy:smith-quality-do-nothing` | confidence: **verified** | tags: global, process, quality, low-turnover

Rule 1 - good companies: high ROCE in cash terms, high gross margins (pricing power), high cash conversion, low leverage, growth that can be reinvested, resilience to obsolescence; avoid banks, heavy cyclicals, airlines, conglomerates. Rule 2 - don't overpay: compare free-cash-flow yield with bond yields and the company's growth. Rule 3 - do nothing: minimise turnover and trading costs; let compounding work. Measured over 2010-2025 the approach beat MSCI World (13.8% vs 12.1% a year) but lagged five calendar years in a row (2021-25), when mega-cap tech concentration, passive flows and de-rating of 'quality defensives' hurt. Indian application: the checklist is close to the Marcellus/consistent-compounder template; the binding constraint in India is rule 2 - quality FMCG/consumer names at 60-80x earnings can deliver low single-digit returns for years even as earnings grow.

body:
**H1 not supported under the pre-registered decision rule. The result looks like a lottery ticket, not a reliable signal.**
351 usable events (2021–2024, ₹500–20,000 cr). Against 5 size-matched random NSE stocks on the same date, the mean
12-month excess was **+6.3%** (95% event-month bootstrap CI **−0.9% to +13.2%**). The **median was −6.9%** (CI −12.8% to −1.5%)
and the **hit rate 43.6%**. The CI includes zero, so the rule says "not supported". The point estimate passes the +5%
"practically relevant" bar with seed 11 but not robustly: seeds 12 and 13 give +5.6% and +4.1%, and both CIs include 0.
The positive mean comes entirely from a right tail. **Dropping the 10 best events turns it into −1.1%.** Most events lag
their controls. Promoter buying sorted the market toward 2021–24's multibaggers (Gallantt, Texmaco Rail, Apar,
Gravita, Titagarh, Jindal Saw…) slightly more often than chance. It did not make the typical pick beat a random
same-size stock.

Compared with the US test (insider_clusters_us.md: 12m 0.0%, CI −4.8 to +5.0), India is directionally more positive, with
the same "mean > 0 > median" shape. That fits the idea that the signal is less arbitraged in India. It is not proof.
title: india_insider_buying › Verdict (short)

body:
- memdb `insight:ownership-disclosure-early-signals` (single-source) treats PIT buying, especially by several KMPs, as an
  informative early signal. **This test does not support that as a return predictor.** KMP buying ≥ ₹1 cr is rare (21 usable
  events) and "≥ 2 buyers" did worse.
- Deuskar, Khatri & Sunder, *Insiders' Other Trades* (ISB/Arizona, NSE-NYU working paper, Apr-2019; BSE 2009–2011,
  SEBI PIT 1992 regime): insiders' own-stock **purchases earn ~3% abnormal over 3 months and ~5.9% over 6 months**, and
  sales earn nothing. Insiders at better-governed firms profit less in their own stock.
  https://archives.nseindia.com/research/content/1718_BS1.pdf (read). Our 3m/6m means are −1.1%/+1.0%, well below those
  figures. Possible reasons: post-2015 PIT regime, the ≥ ₹1 cr filter (larger, more visible promoters), matched-control
  benchmark vs factor models, and publication / free screening.
- IIM Bangalore paper on the 2015 PIT regulations (search snippet only; full text returned 403): own-stock trade
  likelihood and abnormal returns fall after controlling for insider fixed effects, i.e. the 2015 rules appear to have
  worked. https://www.iimb.ac.in/sites/default/files/inline-files/insider-trading-restrictions-informed-trading.pdf. This is
  consistent with a weaker post-2015 signal. Single-source and unread.
- NSE-IGIDR working paper on block trades 2005–15 (search snippet): 3-day CARs positive for insider/promoter block
  purchases. That is a short-window announcement effect and does not contradict a null at 3–12 months.
  https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/research/content/NSE-IGIDR_CG_RPaper_2015-16_WP4.pdf
- US analogue: Lakonishok & Lee (2001), Cohen–Malloy–Pomorski (2012) via memdb `insight:us-insider-buying-evidence`.
  Effects concentrate in small firms and opportunistic insiders.

title: deep_dive_protocol › Synthesis (L7): the override table

body:
1. **Standalone EPS** (D1). For holding-company and group structures this misses subsidiaries. A consolidated re-test from
   FY2020 onward is a natural follow-up.
2. **Price returns** (D3), dividends ignored on both sides. Equal-weighted; no capacity or impact model. ₹500–1,000 cr names can
   cost well over 1% round trip at size.
3. **Sample, not universe:** 580 of ~1,800 companies, so ~50–85 top-quintile names per quarter. A full-universe run would have
   ~2.5× more names per quarter and the same expected effect.
4. **Only 16 quarters per period.** The bootstrap CIs are honest but wide, and one bad quarter (e.g., Mar-2022 −5.4%) moves the
   mean by ~0.6 pp.
5. **Decision-rule edge case:** the long-only rule fails by 0.06 pp on the CI. We report that literally and do not "round up".
6. **Everything in §3 was found after looking at the data.** That includes the mid-tertile strength, the ≥ ₹1,000 cr long-only
   effect, the confirmed-reaction filter and 126d clearing costs. Each needs its own pre-registered test before it is believed.
title: india_pead › 5. Caveats

body:
- **Choose sites to test hypotheses.** Use a mature unit, a new unit in a new geography, and a different format or near-cannibalising unit. Visit off-peak and peak.
- **Count before you talk:** queues, bills per hour, footfall, staff and guards, facings, prices of a fixed basket. Numbers first, opinions second.
- **Talk to five constituencies:** staff, store or plant manager, customers, neighbours/competitors, and a supplier, landlord or driver. Ask about pay, tenure, rent, trips, and switching.
- **Ethics:** identify yourself honestly if asked. Never pay for or solicit confidential or unpublished price-sensitive information (that is insider-information risk). No recordings without consent.
- **Repeat the fixed price basket quarterly.** It is a cheap time series nobody else has.
- **B2B version (v1.1).** Use three visits: (A) an OEM or channel partner and two competitor dealers in the same city, (B) the company's dealer workshop or parts counter, (C) end-users and installers.
  - Count: price sheets *by product node* (same nodes every quarter), price-hike dates and percentages by component, lead times by platform, service bays and jobs, and a fixed basket of 5 spare parts (genuine vs will-fit).
  - Ask end-users the engineering ratio that sizes demand (e.g. DG MW per IT MW).
- **Output:** a "surprises vs model" list. Each model estimate is marked confirmed, contradicted or no read.

body:
1. Adopted: a standing stage-2 size cap. Pledge > 25% or interest cover < 1.5x (non-financials) → starter size
   (proposed 1% of the portfolio at cost), no additions, balance-sheet question. Inside the PEAD avoid window → 0 new
   money (v1.2, unchanged). Interest cover is not applied to lenders (structurally < 1.5x).
2. Not adopted: S1 / S5-India as triggers (no incremental events; no signal alone). They stay "look harder".
3. **Post-hoc, not adopted (future test):** the two triggers behave differently. Pledge is bad on both tails (more
   failures, fewer winners, negative excess in P); interest cover mostly widens the spread (more failures *and* more
   winners in E). A tighter cap for pledge > 50% and a looser one for interest cover alone may fit better — that
   would need its own pre-registration.
4. Proposed code change (not applied): `survival_cap_general_outputs/proposed_card_v1.3.diff` (card + tests;
